Title: Residual perfusion defects in patients with pulmonary embolism are related to impaired fibrinolytic capacity.

Journal/Date: Thrombosis research (2014)

MeSH Keywords: Adult, Aged, Anticoagulants, Biomarkers, Blood Coagulation Tests, Female, Fibrinolysis, Humans


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Few studies investigated the relationship between fibrinolysis abnormalities and residual pulmonary perfusion defects after acute pulmonary embolism (PE).
[OBJECTIVE]: To assess the fibrinolytic profile in patients with prior PE in relation to the extent of scintigraphically detectable residual perfusion abnormalities.
[PATIENTS AND METHODS]: We studied 71 consecutive patients with a prior episode of PE, who were examined after one year of the incident embolic event, and at least one month after anticoagulation withdrawal. They underwent lung scintigraphy to assess the recovery of pulmonary perfusion, echocardiography and chest radiography to look for signs of pulmonary hypertension. Clot formation and lysis were evaluated by two turbidimetric methods: Clot and Lysis Assay and Clot Lysis Time. We also measured the in vitro plasmin-mediated lysis of fibrin from purified fibrinogen, and the circulating levels of fibrinolytic inhibitors. The sample was split in two categories based on the extent of residual perfusion defects: <10% (n=53), ≥ 10% (n=18).
[RESULTS]: Patients with perfusion defects >10% had significantly longer lysis time (p<0.05), and higher levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (p<0.01) than those with perfusion defects <10%. The time interval between symptoms onset and PE diagnosis (time-to-diagnosis) was significantly longer in patients with perfusion defects >10% than in the others (p=0.005). In multivariate logistic regression, both lysis time and time-to-diagnosis were independently associated with perfusion defects >10% (p<0.001). None of the sampled patients had echocardiographic or radiologic signs of pulmonary hypertension.
[CONCLUSION]: Prolonged time-to-diagnosis and fibrinolysis imbalance are independent predictors of incomplete perfusion recovery after acute PE.

--- ABSTRACT ---
The pathophysiology of residual pulmonary vascular obstruction (RPVO) and recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) after unprovoked pulmonary embolism (PE) remains poorly understood. The purpose was to evaluate fibrinolytic and tissue remodeling markers as indicators of RPVO and recurrence after a first unprovoked PE. Analyses were conducted in the 18 to 70-year-old patients included in the PADIS-PE trial, with a pulmonary vascular obstruction (PVO) index ≥ 30% at PE diagnosis. key_findings.finding: Direct human evidence supports an association between impaired fibrinolysis and persistent perfusion defects after acute PE: in a 71-patient follow-up study at 1 year (off anticoagulation), patients with ≥10% scintigraphic residual perfusion defects (n=18) had significantly longer clot-lysis time (p<0.05) and higher PAI-1 (p<0.01) than those with <10% defects (n=53); lysis time and time-to-diagnosis were independently associated with ≥10% defects in multivariable logistic regression (p<0.001). No pulmonary hypertension was present, so this pertains to residual defects rather than established CTEPH.

A prospective observational study of 79 normotensive, noncancer acute-PE patients assessed at admission, 5–7 days, and 3 months, with CT angiographic RPVO at 3–6 months, found RPVO in 23/79 (29.1%). RPVO patients had denser fibrin clots (lower fibrin-clot permeability Ks, p<0.001) and longer clot-lysis time (p<0.05) at baseline and day 5–7; baseline Ks, baseline D-dimer, and 3-month E-selectin were independently associated with RPVO. This supports an association with hypofibrinolytic/prothrombotic clot phenotype, although CLT was not independently reported as an RPVO predictor and the study was not designed to establish causality.

Evidence is not uniformly positive: an ancillary analysis of the PADIS-PE randomized trial included only 23 adults with first unprovoked PE and initial pulmonary vascular obstruction ≥30%; after anticoagulation and warfarin discontinuation, 6 (26%) had RPVO ≥5%. Quantitative D-dimer, tPA, uPA, TFPI and a tissue-factor-based turbidimetric clot-lysis assay were measured, but clot formation/lysis parameters were not associated with RPVO. TGFβ1, not the fibrinolysis measures, was higher in RPVO. Thus, this small study does not replicate the direct fibrinolysis-RPVO association.

A prospective cross-sectional genetic study compared 46 Turkish CTEPH patients with 106 healthy volunteers and found association of the fibrinogen Aα THR312ALA polymorphism with CTEPH (e.g., THR/ALA vs ALA/ALA susceptibility OR 5.026, 95% CI 1.774–14.242; THR/THR vs ALA/THR showed lower susceptibility). VKORC1 and CYP2C9 polymorphisms were not associated. This is indirect thrombophilia/fibrin-structure evidence in established CTEPH, not a direct assay of impaired fibrinolytic capacity or a longitudinal demonstration after acute PE.

Overall conclusion: residual pulmonary perfusion defects/RPVO after PE are plausibly and in several human cohorts associated with impaired fibrinolytic capacity—especially prolonged clot-lysis time, elevated PAI-1, and dense/less permeable fibrin clots—but the evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and partly conflicting. Direct evidence is strongest for residual defects without pulmonary hypertension; evidence in established CTEPH is more indirect and genetic/structural, and available studies do not establish that hypofibrinolysis causes persistent obstruction.

observations: In a prospective cohort of 79 acute PE patients, RPVO occurred in 23/79 (29.1%) at 3–6 months; RPVO was associated with lower fibrin-clot permeability and longer clot-lysis time at baseline and day 5–7.
Baseline clot permeability, D-dimer, and later E-selectin were independently associated with RPVO; the study supports a hypofibrinolytic/prothrombotic clot phenotype but does not establish causality.

source_tools.relevance: Direct prospective evidence linking fibrin structure and lysis resistance to residual pulmonary vascular obstruction.

entities.name: PMID:40544392
observations: In a small PADIS-PE ancillary analysis of 23 patients with first unprovoked PE, quantitative D-dimer, tPA, uPA, TFPI, and tissue-factor-based clot-lysis parameters were not associated with residual pulmonary vascular obstruction; 6/23 had RPVO.
The negative result conflicts with other cohorts but is limited by the small sample and selected population.

source_tools.relevance: Direct negative human evidence regarding measured fibrinolysis parameters and RPVO.

entities.name: PMID:36856592
observations: In a cross-sectional study of 46 CTEPH patients and 106 controls, fibrinogen Aα THR312ALA polymorphism was associated with CTEPH, with one genotype comparison showing OR 5.026 (95% CI 1.774–14.242).
This is indirect evidence compatible with altered fibrin structure or thrombophilia, not a direct functional fibrinolysis assay after acute PE.

source_tools.relevance: Indirect genetic evidence in established CTEPH.

entities.name: Residual PE hypofibrinolysis
observations: Across small human cohorts, residual perfusion defects or RPVO after PE are associated in several studies with prolonged clot-lysis time, elevated PAI-1, or dense less-permeable fibrin clots.
Evidence is heterogeneous and partly conflicting; available studies support association but do not establish that impaired fibrinolysis causes persistent obstruction.

source_tools.relevance: Integrated conclusion from direct positive, direct negative, and indirect studies.
